intro: Artur Schnabel plays the first movement, Allegro assai, of the Piano Sonata No. 23, Op. 57, the “Appassionata”. It begins very softly, with both hands tracing a bare F minor chord, and within a few bars its quietest theme is followed by violent writing.

sections.label: A · Bare octaves in F minor
sections.mNote: A broken chord, then three short notes and a long one.

sections.label: B · Dolce second theme, A♭ major
sections.mNote: A♭ major soon turns to A♭ minor.

sections.label: Dev · Opening theme in E major
sections.mNote: The broken-chord opening theme returns in E major.

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme over repeated C bass
sections.mNote: Repeated bass notes continue beneath the returning theme.

sections.label: B′ · Dolce theme in F major
sections.mNote: The theme returns in F major, then turns to the minor.

sections.label: Coda · Second theme in D♭
sections.mNote: The second theme returns in D♭ before the long slowing.

sections.label: Coda · Più allegro, F minor
sections.mNote: Più allegro in F minor, ending pianissimo.

cues.title: Opening in octaves, F minor
cues.text: The hands play together in octaves, quietly outlining F minor. The same phrase is then repeated a semitone higher. A short repeated-note figure follows, low on the keyboard, made of three short notes and a long one.
cues.evidence: First edition, Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie, plate 521, p. 2, bars 1–17. Harmonic account: https://tonic-chord.com/beethoven-piano-sonata-no-23-in-f-minor-analysis/ . Facsimile: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cranz edition, Hamburg, 1838
cues.text: In 1838, eleven years after Beethoven’s death, the Hamburg publisher Cranz issued a four-hand arrangement under the title Sonata appassionata. The name stuck. Beethoven never wrote appassionato anywhere in the sonata.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus work catalogue, nickname and publication history: https://www.beethoven.de/en/work/view/5292968940404736 . Beethoven died in 1827.

cues.title: Second subject in A♭ major
cues.text: A new melody rises through A♭ major, marked dolce (sweetly), in bars 36–62. It has the broken-chord shape of the opening, now with an accompaniment. A♭ minor takes over within the same passage, and the hands drive towards a much fiercer ending.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 3–4, bars 36–62: dolce second subject in A♭ major and its continuation in A♭ minor.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Development, E major restatement
cues.text: The exposition ends in A♭ minor. The development opens with the bare opening phrase restated in E major, a distant key. Beethoven takes it through further keys, then develops fragments of the second theme.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 4–7, development from bar 66. Tonic Chord identifies the E-major restatement and the use of both principal themes: https://tonic-chord.com/beethoven-piano-sonata-no-23-in-f-minor-analysis/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation over dominant pedal
cues.text: The opening theme returns in F minor at bar 136, over a repeated C in the bass. This dominant pedal moves to D♭ and then back to C.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 8, bars 136–140: return of the first subject over a dominant pedal on C. The pedal subsequently moves to D♭ and back to C.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schnabel leaves Berlin, 1933
cues.text: This recording by Schnabel dates from 1933. That year, with the Nazis in power, he left Germany with his family and settled in Italy. He had made Berlin his home for more than thirty years.
cues.evidence: Schnabel Music Foundation biography: Berlin from 1899, departure with his family in 1933, first to Italy. https://schnabelmusicfoundation.org/musicians/artur-schnabel/

cues.title: Second subject in F major
cues.text: The dolce melody returns in F major. F minor then follows, repeating the change from major to minor that the tune underwent in the exposition.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 9–10, bars 175–201: second subject in F major, followed by its F-minor continuation from bar 191.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, second subject in D♭ major
cues.text: The coda brings back the broken chord of the opening and takes the second theme into D♭ major. Long runs cross the keyboard. Beethoven then marks ritardando and Adagio, with a fermata before the final fast passage.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 10–12: extended coda, second subject in D♭ at bar 211, then ritardando, Adagio and fermata before Più allegro.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Più allegro and coda in F minor
cues.text: Più allegro: faster. The second subject returns in F minor above repeated chords in the left hand. The movement ends quietly in F minor.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 12–13: Più allegro, second-subject material in F minor at bar 241 and final six bars of tonic harmony.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From triplets to a dolce melody
transitions.from: A · Bare octaves in F minor
transitions.to: B · Dolce second theme, A♭ major
transitions.how: The fast triplet figures settle on E♭, the dominant of A♭ major, and diminish. The right hand then plays a connected melody, marked dolce, above a separate accompaniment. Its rising broken chord recalls the shape of the opening.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 3, bars 25–40. Harmonic account: https://tonic-chord.com/beethoven-piano-sonata-no-23-in-f-minor-analysis/

transitions.title: From A♭ minor to E major
transitions.from: B · Dolce second theme, A♭ major
transitions.to: Dev · Opening theme in E major
transitions.how: The exposition closes in A♭ minor. A short link leads to the opening broken chord, now in E major, with the hands again in octaves. The exposition is not repeated, and this phrase begins the development (bars 62–70).
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 4–5, bars 62–70: A♭-minor close and E-major opening of the development.

transitions.title: C pedal beneath the returning opening
transitions.from: Dev · Opening theme in E major
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme over repeated C bass
transitions.how: The development stays on the dominant of F minor in bars 124–140, with diminished harmony and the repeated-note figure sounding against C. The opening phrase returns above the C pedal, which continues underneath it. The pianist plays the octaves of the opening around that sustained bass.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 7–8, bars 124–140: dominant preparation and return above the C pedal.

transitions.title: Second subject returns in F major
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme over repeated C bass
transitions.to: B′ · Dolce theme in F major
transitions.how: In the recapitulation (bars 152–201 in the first edition) the bridge is rewritten to prepare C, the dominant of F. Its quick figures stop, and the dolce melody enters in F major over a moving accompaniment. In the continuation the major third is flattened and the music turns to F minor.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 8–10, bars 152–201: rewritten bridge, F-major second subject and F-minor continuation.

transitions.title: The bass starts the coda again
transitions.from: B′ · Dolce theme in F major
transitions.how: The F minor closing figures diminish, but their running notes continue into the coda, which begins at bar 201. The opening broken chord returns low on the keyboard, and the coda is extended at bar 205. At bar 211 the second tune appears in D♭ major, and both phrases are developed again.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 10–11, coda from bar 201, extended at bar 205; second subject in D♭ major at bar 211.

transitions.title: Fermata on C and the Più allegro
transitions.how: The runs break into short chords, marked ritardando, then Adagio. A fermata holds the dominant harmony over C. The Più allegro opens with chords, and the second theme returns in F minor above a repeated accompaniment in the left hand.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 12: ritardando, Adagio, fermata and Più allegro. Facsimile: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0

fields.note: Inspection of the downloaded selected stream found MP3 audio at 44,100 Hz, two channels and 256,000 bit/s, plus an attached JPEG portrait. Archive calls the file ‘VBR MP3’; that repository format label is distinct from the inspected stream and encoder tag.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: original sound recording first published in 1934.
fields.note: The Public Domain Project release-set catalogue explicitly gives 1934 as the first release of HMV DB 2211–2217; Bloesch identifies Op. 57 within that issue as DB 2215–2217, matrices 2B 6605–6610. Publication is thus documented separately from the 11 April 1933 session. Under the programme’s territorial EU rule, the earlier 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established and no worldwide clearance is claimed. The Archive’s Public Domain Mark is an assertion, not an ownership release; the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not relied upon. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
